en: Vāhaṭa: Having paid homage to the Omniscient One, this glossary (nighaṇṭu) of substances whose names are expressed cryptically, as spoken in the *Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha*, is now being declared. (Vāhanighaṇṭu 1)
Vidārī, pañcāṅgula, vṛścikālī, vṛścīva, devāhvaya, śūrpaparṇī, kaṇḍūkarī, the two known as jīvanāhva and svasaṃjñā, pañcamūlaka, gopasutā, and tripādī constitute five pentads. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 2)
This group, beginning with Vidārī, is pleasing to the heart, nourishing, and subdues wind and bile;
it is a collection that cures consumption, abdominal tumors, body aches, upward breathlessness, and cough. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 3)
Vidārī, gajavājī, iṣṭā, vṛṣagandhā, ikṣugandhikā, śṛgālikā, puṣpavallī, śuklakandā, and palāśikā. (Vanauṣadhisaṃgraha 4)
Kṣīrekṣu, vallīgandhā, kṣīraśuklā, payasvinī, vallīpalāśikā, kṣīravidārī, and śreṣṭhakandaka. // VAnigh_5 //
Pañcāṅgula, vardhamāna, citra, gandharvahastaka,
uruvūka, eraṇḍa, and āmaṇḍa are the destroyers of wind (vāta).
The second is raktairaṇḍa; then vyāghra, which resembles the palm of a tiger;
nakra, ahidaṃṣṭrikā, kolī, vṛścikālī, and uṣṭradhūmaka. (Vāgbhaṭanighaṇṭu 7)
Kāleyī, dhūmrapattra, uṣṭrā, viśalyā, sarpadaṃṣṭrikā, punarnavā, varṣaketu, vṛścīva, and śvetamūlaka. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 8)
Varṣābhū, dīrghapattra, vikasa, kaṭhillaka,
sunāḍika, raktapuṣpa, viśākha, and maṇḍalacchada are synonyms for the plant known as *punarnavā*.
Sahadevā, mahāgandhā, devagandhā, balāhvayā, gāṅgerukī, nāgabalā, kharabandhā, and niśāhvayā. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 10)
Viśvadevā, jhaṣā, kālā, asvagavedhukā, mudgaparṇī, sahā, sūpyaparṇī, and mārjāragandhikā. (Vaijayantī 11)
Kākamudgā and Kṣudrarasā are laxatives that cure hemorrhagic disorders;
Piśācī, Siṃhavinnā, Māṣaparṇī, and Mahāsahā [are also such].
Markaṭī, ātmaguptā, kaṇḍūkṛt, kapikacchurā, vṛṣyabījā, galekaṇḍūkarī, and śārdulavigrahā. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 13)
Phaṇijihvā, parṇī, abhīru, pīvarī, indīvarī, varī, sūkṣmapattrā, dvīpiśatru, śatamūlī, and śatāvarī [are synonyms].
Kākoli, Kavarī, Vīrā, Dhvāṅkṣolī, Kṣīraśuklikā, Jīvantī, Jīvanī, Jīvā, Śākaśreṣṭhā, and Sumaṅgalā. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 15)
Payasyā, payasī, poṭagalā, and jñeyārkapuṣpikā are synonyms;
likewise, jīvaka, kūrcanibha, vṛṣāṇī, vṛṣabha, and vṛṣa are synonyms.
Pṛśniparṇī, pṛthakparṇī, dhāvanī, kalaśī, guhā, śṛgālavinnā, lāṅgūlī, sthirā, and kroṣṭukapucchikā are synonyms. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 17)
Vidārigandhā, aṃśumatī, śālaparṇī, sthirā, dhruvā, triparṇī,
atiguhā, saumyā, mahākṣī, and tanvikā are considered synonyms.
Vyāghrī, nidigdhikā, kṣudrā, drāvaṇī,
kaṇṭakārikā, siṃhā, kṣudravārttākī, bṛhatī, and bahuputrikā are synonyms for the plant *Solanum indicum*.
Vārttākī, hiṅgulī, siṃhī, bhāṇṭākī, duṣpradharṣiṇī, gokaṇṭaka, gokṣuraka, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and trikaṇṭaka. (Vaijayantīkośa 20)
Kanyā, gopī, kṛṣṇavallī, sārivā, phāṇijihvikā, sugandhimūlā, bhadrā, sugandhā, and gopavallī [are synonyms]. (Vaijayantīkośa 21)
Haṃsapādī, raktapādī, tripādī, kīṭamārikā, dhṛtarāṣṭrapadī, and mṛtamandātiparṇikā. (Vaiśeṣikanighaṇṭu 22)
Sārivā, uśīra, kāśmarya, madhūka, the two types of śiśira, yaṣṭīmadhu, and paruṣaka destroy burning sensations, blood-bile disorders, thirst, and fever. (Vāgbhaṭa Nighaṇṭu 23)
I shall now describe the Sārivādi group; first, Sārivā was mentioned [in the previous list], as well as vīraṇī, abhayā, lāmajjaka, uśīra, and amṛṇālaka. (Vaiśeṣikanighaṇṭu 24)
Vīra, vīraṇamūla, bahumūla, raṇapriyā, kāśmarya, abhīru, śrīparṇī, kāśmarya, and likewise kaṭphala. (Vaijayantī-nighaṇṭu 25)
Ḍolāphala, tīkṣṇasāra, madhūka, guḍapuṣpaka, madhupuṣpa, lodhrapuṣpa, vānaprastha, and madhudruma. (Vaijayantī 26)

That which is known as *madhūla* or *madhūka*, growing in water with small leaves and oil-like flowers, should be understood as identical [to the former] in terms of taste and potency. (Vāgbhaṭanighaṇṭu 27)
Bhadraśrī, malayaja, gośīrṣa, śvetacandana, kucandana,
tāmracandana, lohita, and raktacandana.
Yaṣṭīmadhuka, yaṣṭyāhvā, madhuka, and klītakāhvaya are synonyms.
Paruṣaka is called mṛduphala, roṣaja, and dhanvanacchada.

This group, beginning with *kṛṣṇā* (Piper nigrum), consisting of twenty ingredients—namely *kṛṣṇā*, *granthika*, *kākamācī*, *cavikā*, *viśvauṣadha*, *ajājī*, *pāṭhā*, *rāmaṭha*, *reṇukā*, *gajakaṇā*, *siddhārtha*, *citra*, *uṣaṇa*, *spṛkkā*, *jātī*, *ajamoda*, *hiṅgu*, *truṭi*, *bhārṅgī*, and *viḷaṅga*—removes diseases caused by *kapha*. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 30)
Pippalī, māgadhī, kṛṣṇā, vaidehī, capalā, kaṇā,
upakulyā, kaulanāmā, śauṇḍī, and tīkṣṇataṇḍulā are synonyms for long pepper.
Kākamācī has clustered fruits and is beneficial for the voice; maricikā has pepper-like fruits;
kākolī, cavikā, cavya, granthilā, and kolavallikā are [synonyms]. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 32)
Śuṇṭhī, mahauṣadha, viśva, nāgara, and viśvabheṣaja are synonyms for dry ginger.
Ajājī and jīraka are synonyms for cumin; mātā and medhya are synonyms for the cumin from the northern regions (auttarāpatha).
Kṛṣṇajīrā is kākolī; it purifies black eructations.
Jīraṇā is kārabhī, and upakuñcikā destroys pain in the womb.
Mālavī, triśirā, pāṭhā, prācīnā, vṛttaparṇikā, ambaṣṭhā, sthāpanī, vīrā, bodhakī, and kucelikā. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 35)
Hiṅgu is a destroyer of living beings, a digestive aid, a slayer of spirits, and a destroyer of urinary disorders;
reṇukā is also known as kapilā, kauntī, rājaputrī, and hareṇukā.
Gajakaṇā, akṛtrimā, cavikāphala, āsurī, sarṣapa, rājī, and nāsāsaṃvedana are synonyms for the pungent substance known as kaṭu. 37.
Siddhārthaka is the destroyer of spirits (*bhūta*) and a slayer of demons (*rakṣas*); it is also known as white mustard.
Tilā, kaṭvī, matsyapittā, kaṭukā, and śakulādanī [are synonyms]. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 38)
Vallīja and yavaneṣṭa are synonyms for marica (black pepper), which is sharp and pungent.
Spṛkkā, spṛk, brāhmaṇī, devī, piśunā, latā, and satī are synonyms for the same plant.
Jātīphala, majjasāra, jātī, madana, śauṇḍika, ajamodā, kharāhvā, bastamodā, and markaṭī. (Vaijayantīkośa 40)
Elā is drāviḍī and tutthā; sūkṣmailā is bahulā and truṭi; bhārṅgī and gardabhaśāka are synonyms for padmā and brāhmaṇayaṣṭikā.
Padmaka, puṇḍraka, vṛddhi, tugā, ṛddhi, śṛṅgī, and amṛtā—these ten are known as the *jīvana* (life-giving) group.
They increase breast milk, destroy internal heat (*pitta*), and are nourishing, life-sustaining, bulk-promoting, and aphrodisiac.
I shall now describe the *padmakādi* group: *padmaka* is indeed the golden lotus (*hemapadma*).
Prapauṇḍarīka, śrīpuṣpa, and puṇḍrāhva are synonyms for mūlasādhana.
Vṛddhi, śrāvaṇī, puṣṭi, and mahāvṛddhi are said to be synonyms for it;
likewise, tavakṣīrī, tuṣā, śubhrā, vaṃśākhyā, and vaṃśarocanā are its names.
Śṛṅgī is known as Mahāghoṣā; it should be understood that Karkaṭaśṛṅgikā is the same.
Guḍūcī is called Kuṇḍalī, Chinnaruhā, Kāṇḍodbhavā, and Amṛtā. (Vāgbhaṭanighaṇṭu 45)
Madhuparṇī is known as Vayaḥsthā, Maṇḍalī, and Tantrikā;
Śalyaparṇī is Maṇicchidrā; and Medā is Medaḥsamudbhavā.
Mahāmedā, vṛkṣaruhā, and mahāpuruṣadantikā are proclaimed to be the names for the ten life-promoting (jīvanīya) herbs.
Paruṣaka, grapes, kaṭphala, the fruit of the kataka nut,
rājāhva, pomegranate, and śāka vegetables conquer thirst, urinary disorders, and vāta diseases.
I shall describe the *paruṣādi* group; first mentioned is *paruṣaka*, while *varottamā*, *triphalā*, and *śreṣṭhā* are also names for the three fruits (*phalatraya*).
Prāṇadā, Pūtanā, Amoghā, Harītakī, Abhayā, Jayā,
Pathyā, Amṛtā, Haimavatī, Kāyasthā, and Rohiṇī are recorded as synonyms for the myrobalan fruit.
Akṣa, kali, karṣaphala, and vibhītaka are names for the *vibhītaka* tree, which grows on the Vindhya mountains;
it is also called koraṅgaka and mṛduphala. Dhātrī, āmalakī, and śivā are names for the *āmalaka* (myrobalan) tree.
Rohiṇī is said to be khaṭvalā, and drākṣā is likewise mṛduphalā;
mṛdvīkā is uttamaphalā, and gostanī is the variety from the northern region (auttarāpathā).
Hemavalka, mahāvalka, and bhadravṛkṣa are thus proclaimed;
the fruit of the *kataka* tree is known as *kātya*, which clarifies water.
Rājādana, kṣīraśukla, rājāhva, and vānarapriya;
śukeṣṭa, dāḍima, and raktabījaphala—these are the names for the pomegranate.
Svādvamla is appetizing; the second [variety] is Amladāḍima.
Bṛhacchada, Śāka, Varadāru, and Kharacchada are synonyms for it.
Añjana, phalinī, māṃsī, padma, utpala, rasāñjana,
śaila, madhuka, and nāgāhva remove poison, internal burning, and pitta.
Srotoñjana is known as vīra-añjana, as well as yāmuna;
it is also called srotodbhava, nādya, sauvīra, and netrabhūṣaṇa.
Phalinī, kolagirikā, śyāmā, kāntā, priyaṅgukā, piśācī, nalada, māṃsī, jaṭilā, and bhūtakeśinī. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 58)
Nalina, puṣkara, padma, aravinda, kuśeśaya,
paṅkeruha, tāmarasa, sārasa, and sarasīruha are synonyms for lotus.
Bisaprasūna, rājīva, jalaja, and ambhoruha;
indīvara, kuvalaya, nīla, and likewise nīlotpala.
*Saugandhika* is *kalhāra*; *raktotpala* and *sugandhika* are synonyms. *Dravāhva*, *amṛtāsaṅga*, and *kṛta* denote *rasāñjana*, also known as *tārkṣya*.
Elā is said to be drāviḍī, while bahulā is known as truṭi; hemapuṣpa, nāgāhva, kesarā, and nāgakesara are synonyms for nāgakeśara.
Paṭola, kaṭurohiṇī, candana, madhusrava, guḍūcī, and pāṭhā together destroy kapha, pitta, skin diseases, fever, poison, vomiting, loss of appetite, and jaundice. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 63)
The *paṭola* group consists of *rājīmat*, *kulaka*, and *paṭolaka*;
it is also known as *kharacchada*, *pāṇḍuphala*, *rājamānya*, and *amṛtāphala*.
Pīluparṇī is known as madhurasā and mūrvā, which is also called cātirasā;
it is further termed madhusravā, pīlupattrā, moraṭī, and kṣīramoraṭa.
Guḍūcī, padmaka, āriṣṭa, dhānaka, and red sandalwood destroy fever caused by pitta and kapha, vomiting, burning sensations, and thirst; they also stimulate the digestive fire.
Nimba, ariṣṭa, and guḍūcī are among the names for the neem tree; picumanda and śukapriya are also used for it.
Dhānyā, kustumburu, dhānya, dhanikā, and dhānyaka likewise refer to coriander.
Āragvadha, indrayava, pāṭalī, kākatiktā, nimba, amṛtā, madhurasā, sruc, vṛkṣa, pāṭhā;
bhūnimba, sairya, paṭola, the two types of karañja, saptacchada, agni, suṣavī, phala, bāṇa, and ghoṇṭā. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 68)
The group beginning with *āragvadha* conquers vomiting, skin diseases, poisons, and fevers;
it subdues phlegm, itching, and urinary disorders, and serves as a purifier of malignant ulcers. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 69)
Āragvadha, rājavṛkṣa, śamyāka, caturaṅgula, ārevata,
vyādhighāta, pragraha, and kṛtamālaka are synonyms for the same plant.
Kaliṅgaka, indrayava, and vatsaka are synonyms for the fruit of the *kauṭaja* tree;
likewise, pāṭalī, dīrghavṛttā, sthalyā, amoghā, and ambuvāsinī [refer to the same].
Vṛttatuṇḍā, kākatiktā, śārṅgeṣṭā, aṅgāravallikā, vyāghrapāda, sruvataru, svādukaṇṭa, and vikaṅkata.
Kirātatikta, bhūnimba, kattṛṇa, and kāṇḍatiktaka are synonyms.
Sairyaka, sahacara, saryaka, and mṛdupuṣpaka are synonyms.
Bāṇa is known as nīlapuṣpa; it is the lord of firmness, heroism, and fragrance.
Pūtikarañja, kaiḍarya, prakīrya, and cirabilvaka [are synonyms].
Udakīrya, naktamāla, karañja, lājapuṣpaka, saptacchada,
ayugmapattra, saptāhva, and gucchapuṣpaka.
Citraka is also known as dvīpin and is a synonym for fire;
likewise, there is another called raktacitra, as well as mahāṅga and kālamūlaka.
Pānīyavallī, suṣavī, bṛhadvallī, and utpalacchadā; gāla, rāṭha, madana, piṇḍīta, and karahāṭaka.
Śalyaka is the kaiḍarya tree; chardana is the tagara plant; its fruit is called phala;
ghoṇṭā, muṇṭha, and gopaghoṇṭa are synonyms; and padmakī is called markaṭāhvayā.

Asana, tiniśa, bhūrja, śvetavāha, prakīryā, khadira, kadara, bhaṇḍī, śiṃśapā, meṣaśṛṅgī, trihima, tala, palāśa, joṅgaka, śāka, śāla, kramuka, dhava, kaliṅga, chāgakarṇa, and aśvakarṇa. (Vaijayantī 79)
The *asanādi* group overcomes vitiligo, leprosy, phlegm, and worms;
it cures anemia and urinary disorders, and is a destroyer of fat-related defects.
Asana and others: pītasāra, priyaka, bījaka, asana, syandana, stimita, nemi, rathadru, and sarvasādhaka.
Bhūrja, bhurja, bahupuṭa, mṛdutvak,
asthiracchada, pārtha, arjuna, śvetavāha, kakubha, and the one called phālguna [are synonyms for the birch tree].
Gāyatrī, khadira, gītā, kuṣṭhaghna, bālapattraka, kadara, khadira-sāra, koṭarī, and śyāmasāraka. // VAnighaṇṭu 83 //
Bhaṇḍī, śukadru, plavaṃga, śirīṣa, and mṛdupuṣpaka; kapilā, śiṃśapā, kṛṣṇasāra, and maṇḍalapattraka. (Vāhanighaṇṭu 84)
Bastāntrī, meṣaśṛṅgī, cakṣuṣyā, and bahulāṅgikā;
kāleyaka, pītasāra, and the third, varṇakṛt—these are excellent for coloring. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 85)

*Tāḍa*, *tāla*, and *dīrghataru* denote the palmyra tree; *tṛṇarāja* and *tribījaka* denote the date palm; *palāśa*, *kiṃśuka*, *vātarodha*, *brahmataru*, and *paṭu* denote the flame tree (*Butea monosperma*).
Joṅgaka is known as the cooler of cold; agaru is named loha; sajahvi is śrīkara; and śāla, rasa, niryāsa, and rālaka are synonyms.
Dhava is a very hard tree, pale in color, with eyes like those of a cart; it grows in deserts.
Kramuka, kaivuka, pūga, kaṣāya, and madhurāhvaya are synonyms for the betel nut tree.
Śvetaghna, Śītaśamana, Bastakarṇa, Ajakarṇaka,
Śasyasaṃvaraṇa, Śūra, Kuśika, and Aśvakarṇaka.

Varuṇa, the two types of sairyyaka, śatāvarī, dahanā, moraṭa, bilva, viṣāṇikā, the two types of bṛhatī, the two types of karañja, the two types of jayā, and abundant sprouts of darbha grass are the makers of healing. // VAnighaṇṭu 90 //
The group beginning with Varuṇa subdues phlegm, fat, and sluggish digestion;
it also cures Āḍhyavāta, headache, abdominal tumors, and internal abscesses.
Among the *varuṇa* trees and others, the white-flowered variety is known as *varuṇa* or *varaṇa*;
the *śaṭāla* tree is *bilva*, which is not feminine; and *pūtivāta* is the large-fruited tree.
Mālūra, śrīphala, śaiva, śāṇḍilya, śrīnivāsaka,
mahākālyaja, śṛṅgī, kūrcaparṇī, and viṣāṇikā.
Jayā, agnimanthā, araṇikā, तक्कारी (takkārī), and vaijayantikā; śigru, śobhāñjana, tīkṣṇagandha, and bahalapallava. // VAnighaṇṭu 94 //
Muraṅgī, śigruka, and raktapuṣpa are synonyms for madhuraśigruka;
the third is madhura, siṃhakesara, and madhuśigruka.
*Sita*, *tīkṣṇa*, *śigrubīja*, *śvetāṅga*, and *maricāhvaya* are synonyms for white mustard.
*Darbha*, *kuśa*, *lava*, *sthūla*, *sūkṣma*, and *vedapavitraka* are synonyms for *kuśa* grass.
Rujākara, ārtagala, huṃkāra, bhīṣaṇāhvaya,
jālavṛkṣa, and duṣpradharṣa are known as synonyms for the plant with sweet and bitter fruits.
Ūṣaka, tutthaka, hiṅgu, the two types of kāsīsa, saindhava salt, and śilājatu remove urinary disorders, stones, abdominal tumors, obesity, and phlegm. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 98)
In the group beginning with *ūṣaka*, however, there is *vṛṣaka*, *vūṣaka*, and that called *rucaka*;
*ūṣa* is known as *niḥsāraka* and *siṃha*, and it is said to increase the urine.
Kaṭhina, tutthaka, dvedhā, karpara, barhikaṇṭaka, jantughna, jaraṇa, hiṅgu, rāmaṭha, and bhūtanāśana [are synonyms for asafoetida]. 100.
Kāsīsa is called *pāṃśudhāva*, while the second is known as *puṣpa*;
then there are *saindhava*, *māṇimantha*, and *nādeya*, the best of salts.
Śilāja is known to be derived from minerals; śilājatu originates from Mount Mandara.
It is called pārāvata, śailaniryāsa, girija, and by the name śilā. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 102)
Vellantara, araṇika, būkavṛṣa, aśmabheda, gokaṇṭaka, utkaṭa, sahācara, bāṇa, kāśa, vṛkṣādanī, nala, kuśā, dvaya, guṇṭha, gundrā, bhallūka, moraṭa, kuraṇṭaka, rambha, and pārtha. (Vanauṣadhivarga 103)
This section beginning with *vīratara* destroys diseases caused by *vāta*;
it removes urinary stones, gravel, dysuria, and the pain of injuries. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 104)
Vellantara, vīrataru, vīratarādika, vasuka, sthūlapuṣpa, buka, and īśvaramallikā constitute the group beginning with vīratarādika. (Vāhanighaṇṭu 105)
Siṃhāsya, karkaṭa, vṛṣaka,
aṭarūṣaka, veṇupatrī, vṛṣā, pārvī, parvaṇī, and vaṃśapatrikā [are synonyms].
*Aśmabhedin*, *śilābhedin*, and *pāṣāṇabhedikā* are to be known as synonyms for *utkaṭā*.
It has fine leaves and long red stalks. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 107)
*Śara* and *ikṣukusuma* are synonyms for *bāṇa*; its feet resemble the stalks of sugarcane (*kāṇḍekṣu*).
*Kāśa* is called *śvetacāmara*, while *gundrā* is known as *gucchapuṣpikā*.
Vṛkṣādanī, śikhara, vandāka, and kāmavṛkṣaka;
mṛdupuṣpa, suṣira, nadīstha, nalaka, and nala. (Vaijayantī-nighaṇṭu 109)
Guṇṭha, vṛttatṛṇa, śuṇṭha, and śṛṅgaverābhamūlaka; bhallūka, bhūtavṛkṣa, śyonāka, and ṭuṇṭuka.
Śrīhastinī, kuraṭakā, picuka, śitivāraka,
kṛṣṇasūkṣmaphalā, yuktapuṣpā, and mastakamañjarī.
Karambha, Karkaśā, Yugmaphalā, Uttamakanyā, Kapotavaṅkā, Varadā, Ravibhaktā, and Suvarcalā. (Vaijayantī-nighaṇṭu 112)
Rodhra, śābaraka, rodhra-palāśa, jiṅgiṇī, sarala, and kaṭphala; kutsitāmba, kadalī, gataśoka, sailavālu, paripelava, and mocā. 113.

This group, known as the Rodhra-adi (the Rodhra-group), removes fat and phlegm; it cures disorders of the female reproductive tract, is astringent, improves the complexion, and destroys poison. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 114)
In the Lodhra-group, Tilvaka is lodhra, also called tirīṭa and paṭṭikāhvaya;
the second is śābara, white, thick-barked, and known as the medicine for the eyes (akṣibheṣaja).
*Jiṅgiṇī* and *jhiṅgiṇī* are known as *mocakī* and *guḍamañjarī*;
*pūtikāṣṭha* is *devavṛkṣa*, and *sarala* is *devadāruka*.
Surakāṣṭha and bhadradāru are synonyms for the deity;
sugandhā, suvahā, and rāsnā are synonyms for yuktāhvā and gandhanākulī.
The *surabhi*, the *kadamba*, the *kuñcitāṅga*, and the *haripriya*;
the *rambhā* is the *kadalī*, also called *mocā*, having round flowers and sun-like fruits.
Aśoka, vigataśoka, subhaga, and tāmrapallava;
elavāluka, aileya, bāleya, and harivāluka. (Vāhanighaṇṭu 119)
Kuṭannaṭa, plavaṅga, vitunna, and paripelava;
surabhi, sallakī, mocā, mahārambhā, and gajapriyā. (Vaijayantī-nighaṇṭu 120)
Arka, ālaka, nāgadantī, viśalyā, bhārṅgī, rāsnā, vṛścikālī, prakīryā, pratyakpuṣpī, pītatailodakīryā, the two types of śvetā, and the tree of the ascetics (tāpasavṛkṣa). 121.
This group of plants beginning with arka removes phlegm, fat, and poison;
it pacifies worms and skin diseases, and especially purifies wounds. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 122)
In the *Arkādi* group, *sadāpuṣpā*, *sūryāhvā*, and *arka* refer to the *rūpikā* plant;
while *mandāra*, *śvetakusuma*, *alarka*, and *vikaraṇa* are recorded as synonyms for it.
Nāgadantī, śvetaghaṇṭā, nāginī, pūrvapuṣpikā,
viśalyā, halinī, vahnijihvā, and lāṅgalikā are known [as synonyms].
Bhārṅgī, phaṇjī, pālindī, dvijayaṣṭi, and sugandhikā; apāmārga, śaikharika, pratyakpuṣpī, and mayūraka. (Vaiśeṣikanighaṇṭu 125)
Kākādanī, pītatailā, vegā, and likewise kākāṇḍakī;
jyotiṣmatī, pītatailā, vegā, and kaṅguṇikā are recorded as synonyms.
Śvetā, sunābhi, kaṭabhī, kiṇihī, madhureṇukā, kaṭaṃbharā, mahāśvetā, kālindī, and sitakaṭabhī are synonyms. (Vācaspatyam 127)
Kumārī, Mahāśvetā, Vandhyā, Karkoṭakī, Iṅguda, Tiktamañjā, Pīluka, and Tāpasadruma; // VAnigh 128 //

Surasā, yuga, phaṇijjaka, kālamālā, viḍaṅga, kharabusa, vṛṣakarṇī, kaṭphala, kāsamarda, kṣavaka, sarasī, bhārṅgī, kārmuka, kākamācī, kulaha, viṣamuṣṭi, bhūstṛṇa, and bhūtaveśī. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 129)
The group beginning with *surasā* destroys phlegm, fat, and worms;
it cures catarrh, loss of appetite, dyspnea, and cough, and it purifies wounds. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 130)
In the group beginning with *surasā*, there are two kinds of *surā*:
the black variety (*kṛṣṇagarur*) and the *tulasī* which has sweet-smelling leaves and resides in the body (*kāyasthā*).
Phaṇijjaka, mañjarīka, tīkṣṇagandha, sugandhika, kṛṣṇasarjaka, kālamāla, vaṭhiñjara, and kuṭheraka. (Vaijayantīkośa 132)
Viḍaṅga is known as kṛmijit, balya, kirīṭa, and śvetataṇḍula;
śūkātmaka, kharabusa, maruva, and kharapatraka are synonyms for it.
Vṛṣakarṇī, ākhukarṇī, and likewise bhūmipariśrayā;
rājakṣava and pītapuṣpa; and kāsamardaka, which destroys cough (kāsaghna).
Udvegajanana, tīkṣṇa, kṣavaka, and kṣudvibodhaka;
kapitthapattrī, jharasī, nirjharā, and jharapattrikā. (Vaiśampāyana-nighaṇṭu 135)
Prācīnā, bodhakī, kāntā, kāmukā, and raktamañjarī are synonyms for the *mādhavī* creeper; it is also called amukta, suvasanta, and atimuktaka.
*Kākamācī* is also called *gūḍhaphalā*, *kākāhvā*, and *mācikā*;
*vola* is *vṛddha*, *kulahala*, *jambūla*, and *bhūkadambaka*.
Viṣamuṣṭi, karkoṭī, kṣayāhvā,
keśamuṣṭikā, putrāñjali, bhūtakeśī, bhūstṛṇa, and guhyabījaka are synonyms for the plant known as *kṣaya*.
Bhūtāveśī, bhūtakeśī, nirguṇḍī, tinduvāraka,
śephālikā, and śvetapuṣpā are known as śvetanirguṇḍikā.
Muṣkaka, snuhī, varā, dvīpī, palāśa, dhava, and śiṃśapā conquer urinary disorders,
urinary gravel, jaundice, obesity, hemorrhoids, kapha, and semen-related ailments.
In the group beginning with *muṣkaka*, however, *śikharī*, *muṣkaka*, and *mokṣaka* are synonyms;
it is also known as *kālamuṣka*, *kṣāravṛkṣa*, and *kṣīṇavāriphala*.
Sudhā, vajrī, mahāvṛkṣa, granthilā, snug, guḍā, snuhī, samantadugdhā, śvajihvā, patra, and yugmakaṇṭaka; // VAnigh 142 //
Vatsaka, mūrvā, bhārṅgī, kaṭukā, marīca, ghuṇapriyā, gaṇḍīra,
elā, pāṭhā, jājī, kaṭvaṅgaphala, ajamoda, siddhārtha, vacā, jīraka,
hiṅgu, viḍaṅga, paśugandhā, and pañcakolaka destroy [the aforementioned ailments].
It cures disorders of wind, phlegm, fat, catarrh, abdominal tumors, fever, colic, and hemorrhoids.
*Vatsakādi* (the group beginning with *vatsaka*) contains *vanatikta*,
*kuṭaja*, *girimallikā*, *vṛkṣaka*, *śakravṛkṣa*, as well as *vatsaka* and *kuṭaja*.
Bhaṅgurā, ativiṣā, mādrī, śuklakandā, and ghuṇapriyā are synonyms;
the second type, however, is considered prativiṣā, śvetaviṣā, and raktaviṣā.
Dīrghavṛnta, mahānimba, kaṭvaṅga, and aralu are synonyms for tiktaka;
dīpyaka and ajamoda are synonyms, while yavānī is called jaraṇā.
Vacā is known as ugragandhā, jaṭilā, ṣaḍgranthā, and haimavatī;
that which is white is called svādukandā, suvāsā, and himasaṃbhavā.
Vacā, jalada, devāhva, nāgara, ativiṣā, amaya, the two types of haridrā, yaṣṭyāhva, kalaśī, and kuṭaja. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 149)
The groups of drugs beginning with vacā and haridrā destroy diarrhea caused by undigested matter (āmātīsāra);
they eliminate disorders of fat (medas), phlegm (kapha), wind (pavana), and defects of the breast milk (stanya). 150.
Regarding the group beginning with vacā: first vacā is mentioned; mustā is called jalada;
gāṅgeyī, kuruvindā, and devāhvā are synonyms for bhadramustaka.
I shall now describe the group beginning with *haridrā*: *gaurī*, *śyāmā*, *nirviṣā*, *niśā*, *kṣapā*, *rātri*, *varā*, and *lomaśamūlikā*. (Vāgbhaṭanighaṇṭu 152)
Svarṇavarṇā, haridrā, niśāhvā, rajanī, dārvī, kaṭaṅkaṭerī, parjanyā, and pacampacā are synonyms for turmeric.
Priyaṅgu, puṣpāñjana, the pair [of] padmas, padmākara-dust, yojanavallī,
anantā, mānadruma, mocarasa, samaṅgā, punnāga, and śīta are the causes for aphrodisiacs.
Ambaṣṭhā, madhuka, namaskarī, the bark of the nandīvṛkṣa, palāśa, kacchurā, rodhra, dhātakī, bilva, peśikā, kaṭvaṅga, and the pollen produced from the lotus. (Vāgbhaṭanighaṇṭu 155)
The two groups beginning with priyaṅgu and ambaṣṭhā destroy chronic diarrhea;
they are healing for the joining of tissues, beneficial for bile disorders, and also promote the healing of wounds.
In the *priyaṅgvādi* group, *priyaṅgu* was mentioned first;
then *padmā*, *asitāravindā*, *cāraṭī*, and *padmacāriṇī*.
*rajaḥ*, *parāgaḥ*, *kiñjalkam*, and *kesaram* denote the filament produced from a lotus;
*mañjiṣṭhā*, *vijayā*, *raktā*, *samaṅgā*, and *vikasāruṇā* denote the plant *Rubia cordifolia*.
Mañjukā, raktayaṣṭī, tāmrā, and yojanavallī;
also anantā, dīrghamūlā, samudrānta, and yavāsaka.
Sāradru, śālmalī, mocā, purāṇī, and raktapuṣpikā are synonyms for the silk-cotton tree;
the resin of the śālmalī is known by the name mocarasa.
Samaṅgā, śatapattrā, likewise añjalikārikā,
namaskārī, raktamūlā, and also puṣpāvarodhikā.
Puṃnāga, puruṣāhva, tuṅga, raktakesara, nameru,
devapuṃnāga, skandhapuṣpa, and surāhvaya are synonyms for the same tree.
Sindhupuṣpī, dhātakī, madayantikā, kuñjarā, harisārā, madavīryā, and madapriyā are synonyms for madahetu (the cause of intoxication).
Ambaṣṭhā is recorded as being found in Ambaṣṭha and other regions; it is also known as sahasrī and bahumūlaka.
Madhuparṇī, kekiśikhā, mayūrāhvā, śikhī, and likewise śikhi [are synonyms].
Nandīvṛkṣa, prarohī, jayavṛkṣa, indravṛkṣaka,
kacchurā, paṇihārī, tīkṣṇapattrā, and marudbhavā.

Mustā, vacā, agni, the two types of niśā, dvitiktā, bhallātaka, pāṭhā, triphalā, viṣā, kuṣṭha, kuṭī, and haimavatī destroy diseases of the female reproductive tract and the breasts, and they are purgatives of impurities. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 166)
In the group beginning with *mustā*, *mustā* itself has already been proclaimed;
it is known to be bitter and pungent. *Rohiṇī* and *kaṭurohiṇī* [are also included].
Bhallātaka, known as aruṣkara, causes eruptions, swellings, and wounds; likewise, pākala, vāri-bhāvya, vāpya, kuṣṭha, and gadāhvaya [are used]. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 168)

Nyagrodha, pippala, sadāphala, the two types of rodhra, the two types of jambu, arjuna, kapītana, somavalka, plakṣa, āmra, vañjula, piyāla, palāśa, nandī, kolī, kadamba, virala, madhuka, and madhūka. (Vaidyanighaṇṭu 169)
The group beginning with Nyagrodha is beneficial for wounds, astringent, a healer of fractures,
and a destroyer of fat, bile, blood disorders, thirst, burning sensations, and diseases of the female reproductive tract.
The *nyagrodha* and others are the abodes of yakṣas; the *nyagrodha* has many roots and is called *vaṭa*.
The *aśvattha*, *pippala*, and *bodhi* are the sacred fig tree (*caityadru*) with trembling leaves.
The udumbara has worm-filled fruit, is well-established, and bears fruit at all times;
the rājajambū has large fruit, while the kākajambū has small grain-like fruit.
Phalaśreṇī, vara, kapicūta, and kapītana are said to be synonyms for the *kapittha* tree.
Plakṣa, kupippala, plāva, gardabhāṇḍa, and kapītana are synonyms for the *plakṣa* tree.
Āmra, cūta, āvatala, kānta, piṇḍaphala, vasantadūtī, mākaṃda, bhṛṅgeṣṭā, and kokilapriyā are synonyms for the mango tree.
Rasāladru, sahakāra, saurabha, and kokilapriya are synonyms for the mango tree;
nādeya and vañjula are said to refer to the same, while vidula and vetasa denote another variety.
Priyāla has a rough trunk and is fond of grape juice;
karkandhū is kāṣṭhakṛt; kolī is badarī, which has paired thorns.
Visphūrjanī, vikaraṇī, tindukī, and viralā are recorded [as synonyms].
Kālaskandha and nīlasāra are known as the second variety, kākatinduka.
Vakraśalyā, kṛṣṇaphalā, viralā,
gṛdhranakhy, gandhayuktā, sāravastrā, durdharṣā, and kuṇḍalī are recorded [as synonyms].

Elā, yugma, turuṣka, kuṣṭha, phalinī, māṃsī, jalada, dhāmaka, spṛkkā, coraka, coca, pattra, tagara, sthauṇeya, jātī, rasa, śukti, vyāghranakha, amarāhva, aguru, śrīvāsaka, kuṅkuma, caṇḍā, guggulu, devadhūpa, khapura, punnāga, and nāgāhvaya. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 179)
The group beginning with Ela (elādi) pacifies wind and phlegm, neutralizes poison,
clarifies the complexion, and destroys itching, pustules, and urticaria.
Elā and the others have been described previously; now another variety, *sūkṣmailā*, is being told:
*bhadrailā*, *bṛhadelā*, and *sthūlailā* are those produced from the *tripuṭa* plant. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 181)
Suhelā, Suṣeṇī, Reṇukā, Kāntanāmikā, Piṇḍī, Turuṣkaja, Taila, Pirāyāka, Kṛtrima, and Kapi. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 182)
Hrīvera, vāri, keśāhva, udīcya, bālaka, jalam, dhyāmaka, śabala, gandha, spṛkkā, devī, latā, and satī [are synonyms for the plant known as *spṛkkā*]. // VAnighaṇṭu 183 //
Coraka is granthiparṇī; śaṭī is somasamudbhavā.
Varāṅga is carmanāmā, and coca, tvak, and varāṅgaka are synonyms for cinnamon bark.
Romasha is the leaf (chadana) or leaf (pattra); Tamala is the romashiphala;
Bahistha is Tagara; and Vakra, Nata, and Kalanusari are synonyms for the same. 185.
Cāraṭī, śukabarha, sthauṇeya, tailapītaka, jātīrasa, rasa, bola, śukti, kararuha, and nakha. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 186)
Badarīpattraka, as well as Nāgahanu, should be known;
Samudraja is to be understood as Vyāghranakha, which bears the name "tiger."
Śrīveṣṭaka is also known as vāyasaka and dadhināman;
kāśmīra, kuṅkuma, rakta, vāhlīka, and ghusṛṇa are celebrated as synonyms for saffron.
Krodhanā, Piśunā, Caṇḍā, Corī, and Śaṅkhinikā are considered [the five types of] sulphur.
Mahiṣākṣa, Niśācārī, Kauśika, Guggulu, and Pura [are the five types of bdellium]. VAnigh 189.
Rāla is known as devadhūpa; śāla is called sarjarasa; and kunduru, medaka, kundra, and khapura are to be understood as synonyms.

Śyāmā, dantī, dravantī, kramuka, kuṭaraṇā, śaṅkhinī, carmasāhvā, svarṇakṣīrī, gavākṣī, śikhari, rajanaka, chinnarohā, karañja, bastāntrī, vyādhighāta, bahala, bahurasa, and the fruits of tīkṣṇavṛkṣa—this group known as Śyāmādi destroys abdominal tumors (gulma), irregular appetite, phlegm, heart disease, and dysuria. *Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 191*
Masūravidalā, śyāmā, śyāmāda, kālameṣikā, suṣeṇikā, śaśāhvā, kālindī, and kālikā are recorded as synonyms.
Citrā, mukūlaka, dantī, nikumbha, and likewise śambara;
udumbaracchadā, hastidantī, and upacitrakā are synonyms.
Nyagrodhāhvā, sutatreṇī, dravantī, undurukarṇikā,
kumbhastrī, bhaṭṭinī, sūtrā, śyāmā, kuṭaraṇā, and trivṛt are synonyms for Trivṛt.
Śaṅkhinī, tiktalā, vakrī, yavatiktā, kiśorikā,
śaṅkhāvartā, śaṅkhapuṣpī, viśikhā, and nāhikā are recorded as synonyms.
Sātalā, saptalā, carmakasā, and āvartakī are recorded [as synonyms];
likewise, brāhmī is celebrated as having the name of Brahmā.
Svarṇakṣīrī, haimavatī, kaṅkuṣṭha, tīkṣṇadugdhikā, indravāruṇikā, aindrī, gavākṣī, and gajacirbhiṭī. (Vaiśeṣikanighaṇṭu 197)
Viśālā, viśalyā, and gavādanī are said to be the same;
likewise, girikarṇī, aśvakṣuraka, and sthāṇukarṇī are synonyms for gavādanī.
Nīlasyandā, nīlapuṣpī, nīlākhyā, and girikarṇikā; tilvaka, śikharī, śvetatvak, tirīṭa, and bṛhacchada.
Kampillaka, rañjanaka, recana, and raktacūrṇaka; bastāntrī, vṛṣagandhā, meṣāntrī, and vṛṣapattrikā. (Vāgbhaṭa’s Nighaṇṭu 200)
The sugarcane (*ikṣu*) has thick and abundant juice; it is called *guḍamūla* and *asipattraka*.
The *śaṇa* is a sharp tree, while the *pīlu* and the other known as *sthāṇuka* are likewise mentioned.

Those substances which belong to the groups (gaṇas), whether in their full collection or in a condensed collection, have been mentioned; hereafter, those that are scattered [throughout the text] will be described.
The *śamī* tree has sacred leaves (*pavitrapattrā*), is auspicious (*maṅgalyā*), and is the goddess Lakṣmī herself; it removes hair defects (*keśanut*).
The *sohalā*, *rudatī*, *tanvī*, and *sūkṣmamūlā* are synonyms for *aparājitā*.
The *pānīya* is a seed-tree, while the *jīvavṛkṣa* is a noose-tree;
the *śaṅkhapuṣpikā* has white flowers, clings to the ground, and has short limbs.
Sarpagandhā has fine leaves; Sarpākṣī has red flowers;
another variety with a very large bulb is Nākulī, which is dear to the mongoose.
Viṣṇukrāntā, nīlapuṣpī, satīnā, and chardikā; likewise vāṭyālaka, pītapuṣpa, vāṭyā, bhadraudanī, and balā. (Vaiśeṣikanighaṇṭu 206)
Mahābalā, varṣapuṣpī, śītapākī, subījaka, vāṭyāyanī, atibalā, bhāradvājī, and suparṇikā are synonyms. (Vaiśeṣikanighaṇṭu 207)
The plant known as *vāṭyā* or *kārpāsā*, which has beautiful blossoms and bears fruit,
is also called *ajaṭā*, *bahupattrā*, *bhūdhātrī*, and *tāmalakī*.
Parpaṭaka has a cooling potency; it quenches thirst and has fine leaves.
Trāyantī and trāyamāṇā are protectors that destroy fear.
Durālabhā, dhanvayāsa, yāsa, duḥsparśaka, kalyāṇalocana, nādeya, and jalajambuka are to be known [as synonyms]. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 210)
Mahākadamba, nicula, anapāyin, jalanūpura, kiṅkirāta, karṇikāra, gaura, and kanakapuṣpaka.
Mandāra is known as Pāribhadrāhvaya, Kaṇṭakī, Kiṃśuka, Pārijāta, Rohīta, Plīhaghna, and Raktapuṣpaka. (Vaijayantī-nighaṇṭu 212)
Śukanāsā is a tube, while śukaghrāṇa is a small tube;
śākarāja is bhūtavāsa, and gojihvā has rough leaves.
Goat’s milk destroys wounds; *phalguvāṭikā* cures leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).
*Siṃhāsya*, *karkaṭa*, *vṛṣa*, *vāsā*, and *āṭarūṣaka* [are likewise medicinal]. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 214)
*Aśmantaka* is known as *amlayoni* and *yamalapattraka*;
*vaṃśa*, *veṇu*, *yavaphala*, *suparvā*, and *tṛṇadhvaja* [are synonyms for bamboo].
The *karīra* is known as the *kīcaka*, the sprout of the fruit of death;
the *vāraṇa*, the *taralī*, the *kumbhī*, the *karañja*, and the *tīravṛkṣaka*. (Vācaspatyam 216)
Sindhura, sindhuvāra, śvetapuṣpa, avarohita, kākodumbarikā, phalgu, bhadrodumbara, and vāyasī.
Kālāntradārī, kanthārī, phaṇī, khadiravallī, sitā, kumārikā, mallī, mohinī, and vaṭapattrikā.
Phenila, hastikarkoṭa, kāṇḍa, bāṇa, and śaṇa are recorded as synonyms.
Śleṣmāntaka, bahuphala, śailūṣa, and kāntavṛkṣaka [are synonyms for the same plant].
Kuddālaka, kovidāra, tāmrapuṣpa,
yugacchada, kālakarṇī, bhūtavallī, balyā, gandhā, and aśvagandhikā.
The *tintiḍīka* is the *vṛkṣāmla*; the *badarī* is known as *kola*. The *karkandhū* is the small *badarī*. The *vasuvṛkṣa*, however, is the *dhanvana*.
Amlavetasa possesses a thousand-fold potency and is pungently sour;
it is also known as varāmla, godhāpadī, godhavallī, paṭvamlā, and ādityanāmikā.
Pattrabhaṅga, mahāśyāmā, kharāśvā, vṛddhadāruka, dāvāgnidamanī, mātā, and likewise kṣudrakaṇṭarikā. (Vaidyanighaṇṭu 223)
Barhiśikhā, guñjā, raktikā, kākaṇantikā,
śvetakāmbhojikā, dhvāṅkṣī, śvetapākī, and śikhaṇḍikā are synonyms for the gunja berry.
The third is *kṛṣṇakāmbhojī*, *kuṇapokā*, *susādanī*, *jyotiṣmatī*, *kaṅguṇikā*, and *pārāvatapadī*. (Vaiśeṣikanighaṇṭu 225)
Īśvarī, nāgadamanī, kīṭāri, and sarpagandhikā;
adhomukhā, avākpuṣpī, vārāhī, and vanamālikā. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 226)
Ārāmaśītala, Deva, Gandhāḍhya, Kurumardaka, Nāgajihvā, Śvetaphalā, Kṣīriṇī, and Arkapuṣpikā. (Vāgbhaṭanighaṇṭu 227)
Nimbacchada, indravallī, karabhī, and rucirā are recorded; likewise, likhikā, bhaktikā, bhūrī, and navanītā are proclaimed.
Jñeyā, badarikāparṇī, parṇaka, pūtikarṇaka, malayū, vākucī, candrarekhā, and avalguja are to be known [as synonyms]. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 229)
Cakṣuṣyā and āraṭī are to be known as such, as is araṇyakulatthikā;
ahimāra is arimeda, while pītadāru is haridruma.
Śvetatvak, tīkṣṇasāra, vibudha, tīkṣṇasāraka,
vāpyāhva, pauṣkara, śūlahara, and bījāhvaya are considered synonyms [for the same plant].
Śarī is to be known as having excellent vows; gandhāhvā and somasambhavā are synonyms for it.
Sahasravīryā, golomī, sitā, dūrvā, and śādvala are names for the same plant.
Kṣudravārī, dugdhayutā, ghaṭikā, chatrapattraka, āghoṭaka, brahmaphala, raktabindu, and tilacchada; // VAnighaṇṭu 233 //
Ajākṣī and lomaparṇī are known as meṣavilocana;
mahāvṛkṣa and mahānīla are remembered as bhṛṅga and mārkava.
Bhṛṅgarāja and bhṛṅgareṇuka are known as keśarañjanaka (hair-dye).
Rāmāhvā, karkatārā, rāmā, taruṇī, and puṣpavatī are synonyms for [the plant] rāma. 235.
Sūryabhaktā, Sukhodbhavā, Sūryāvartā, Ravipriyā,
Hiraṇyapuṣpī, Kharjūrī, Tāḍapatrī, and Musalī are synonyms [for the plant *Butea monosperma*].
Ikṣvālikā, kākekṣu, kāṇḍekṣu, vāyasekṣuka, śvetacāmaraka, kāśa, and likewise ikṣukusuma; these are synonyms for the sugar-cane.
*Adhyaṇḍa*, *ikṣuraka*, *sthūlakaṇṭaka*, and *kokilākṣaka* are known as *uccaṭā* and *caṭakā*; *śikhaṇḍī* is recorded as *āsphotaka*.
Unmattaka, mātulaka, dhuttūra, and heman are synonyms;
tripuṣpa, kṛṣṇadhuttūra, kṛṣṇapuṣpī, and mohinī refer to the black variety.
Devadālī, karkoṭī, veṇī, and jīmūtaka are recorded [as synonyms].
Dhāmārgava, kośaphala, and rājakośātakī are recorded [as synonyms].
Kaṭukośātakī, kṣveḍā, jālinī,
kṛtavedhana, kaṭukālāmbunī, tumbā, alāmbu, and ikṣvākusaṃjñikā are synonyms.
*Nīlinī* is known as *cāraṭī*, and *nīlinī* has blue flowers;
*sūkṣmapāda* and *tāmracūḍa* are known as *kukkuṭapādika*.
Godhūlikā, gojihvā, gojī, kroṣṭukamūlaka,
aṅkola, girikola, pītasāra, and nikocaka.
Jālāri, mehaśatru, bakulī, talapoṭaka,
svarṇavarṇākara, pītapuṣpaka, and dohaka are its names.
Śaṇapuṣpī, bṛhatpuṣpī, and śaṇa are known as ghaṇṭaśaṇa;
both atasī and rudrapattrī are known as gopikā and bāṇaka.
*Saumyā*, *suvarcalā*, *brāhmī*, *somā*, and *brahmasuvarcalā*;
*maṇḍūkaparṇī*, *vikrāntā*, and another *brāhmī* are forest herbs.
Sutajīva, putrajīva, pavitra, putrasiddhikṛt,
āvartakī, carmaraṅgā, mahājālī, and vibhāṇḍikā.
Prasāraṇī, suprasarā, sāraṇī, and supratānikā are synonyms;
while hiṅgupattrī, pṛthvīkā, bāṣpikā, and kavarī are recorded as names for the same plant.
Tumburu, tīkṣṇavalka, tīkṣṇapattra, kutumburu, akṣoḍa, and parvatīya; these are the fruit-oils that depend upon molasses.
It is known as *kīreṣṭa*, *karparāla*, *svādumañjā*, *pṛthucchada*, *agastika*, *munināmā*, and *kumbhayoni*. (Vaijayantīkośa 250)
*Adhicchatrā*, *kumbhayoni*, *droṇapuṣpī*, and *kutumbikā*; and *kauṇḍinya*, *mahādroṇa*, and *devakutumbaka* are recorded [as synonyms]. (VAnighaṇṭu 251)
Adhicchatrā, gautamasthā, and bālagranthi are proclaimed [as synonyms]; vatsādanī is known as sudaśā; and cakrāṅgī is jalaśoṣaka.
Prapunnāṭa, eḍagaja, dadrughna, and cakramardaka;
likewise, lakṣmaṇā, putrajananī, and raktabinducchadā.
Nāginī, śūlinī, and nāgavallī are known as matsyārjaka;
śṛgālaghaṇṭā, vajrākṣī, vajravallī, and śṛṅkhalā [are synonyms].
Palankaṣā, mūlaka, hiṅgu, and puṣkaracchada; dadhipuṣpī, khaṭvāṅgī, khaṭvā, and paryaṅkapādikā. (Vaijayantī 255)
Bimbī, gohā, tuṇḍikerī, and tilākhyā are synonyms for phalanābhikā;
urvāru is called karkaṭī and is also celebrated as lomaśā.
The *khūrjarika* is from Kaliṅga; the *trapusa* is known to be diuretic (*mūtrala*);
the *kūṣmāṇḍakī*, the *puṣpalatā*, and the *kakubhāṇḍa* are considered the best among fruits.
Gorakṣatumbī, gorakṣī, kumbhālāmbu, and ghaṭābhidhā are synonyms;
cirbhiṭikā and citraphalā are also known as cīnāra and cirbhaṭa.
Lambā, Piṇḍaphalā, Ikṣvākū, Kaṭukā, Kṣatriyātmajā, Mahāphalā, Ikṣurā, Tumbikā, and Tiktabījakā. (Vaiśyanighaṇṭu 259)
Cukrikā, āmlikā, ciñcā, jīvantī, and tintiḍī are known as synonyms.
Cukrikā, however, is also called amlacāṅgerī and suniṣaṇṇadalā. (Vaiśeṣika-nighaṇṭu 260)
Upodaka, upodī, kṣudrakā, and likewise podakī;
jīvantika, raktaśāka, kalambī, and vallyupodaka.
Taṇḍulīya, meghanāda, and cillī are known as lomaśā;
śitivāra, sūcipattra, svastika, and suniṣaṇṇaka [are synonyms].
Matsyākṣika, matsīra, pattūra, and priyasā are synonyms;
so too are śīghraśākhā, śākhinī, mahāśāka, and vāstukī.
Śrāvaṇī is known as muṇḍitikā, bhikṣu, and śravaṇaśīrṣakā;
it is also remembered as saumyagandhā, barbarikā, and tilaparṇī.
*Sarpa* is variegated and blue-black in appearance; *bhūśāka* is the bulbous root of the ground (*bhūmikandaka*).
*Rasona* is known as garlic (*laśuna*), while *palāṇḍu* is that which causes foulness of the mouth.
Śatapuṣpā, śatacchattrā, miśi, ghoṣā, śatāhvayā,
miśreyā, śālinī, śītā, śivā, araṇyā, and miśi are recorded as synonyms for the plant known as Miśi.
Pṛthvīkā, vāripattrā, bāṣpikā, and sthalodbhavā; kapittha, dadhittha, durmada, and surabhicchada. (Vaijayantī-nighaṇṭu 267)
Toyakṣobhakara, Kumbhī, Vāruṇa, Vṛkṣadhūmaka,
Mūṣikāri, Citraphala, and Karaṇḍaphalaka— these are its names.
Coca, ciṣu, nārikela, tuṅgadru, kūrcaśekhara, nīrapūrṇaphala, and śṛṅgī are synonyms for the coconut. Moca, however, refers to the fruit of the plantain tree (kadalī).
Rambhā, kadalī, and mocā are synonyms for the plantain tree, which has round flowers and sun-like fruits.
Karamardī is also called kṣīraphalā and śvetapuṣpaphalā; it has white flowers and fruit.
The *karamardaka* has black, ripe fruit and causes distress; it is sour.
The *mātuluṅga*, *bījapūra*, and *luṅga* are synonyms for the *phalapūraka*.
Jambīra, jambhala, jambha, jamba, and dantaśaṭha are known as synonyms for the citron tree.
The orange tree, however, is called tvaksugandha, and it is dear to Airāvata and Mukha.
Bhavya, bhaviṣya, āmla, bhava, and romaphala are considered synonyms.
Pārāvata and raivataka refer to the *likuca* fruit, which is also called *lakuca* and *ḍahu*.
The *panasa* is known as the thorny-fruited jackfruit tree; the *coca* is remembered as the long-fruited tree. The *nalikā* is the hollow, empty reed, also called *kapotacaraṇā* and *naṭī*.
The *snigdhavṛkṣa* is the milky fig tree (*plakṣa*), also known as *guḍabījaka*.
The *kālavṛntā*, *kuberākṣī*, *kuliṅgākṣī*, and *yakṣadṛk* are synonyms for it.
Ugrakāṇḍa, kāravallī, toyavallī, sukāṇḍakā, pañcāṅgulī, liṅgabījā, rājikā, and piṇḍavatphalā. (Vaiśyanighaṇṭu 276)
Turyatuṇḍī, śilācchedī, pūtikā, nityapuṣpikā, parvamañjarikā, kīṭahantrī, and vṛścikahāriṇī. (Vaijayantīkośa 277)
Kumārī, vyāghracaraṇā, kanyā, and sthūladalā; bandhūka, bandhujīva, pārvaka, and vṛkadhūmaka. (Vaijayantī-nighaṇṭu 278)
*Kṛṣṇanīla*, *kālaśākha*, *kaiḍarya*, and *surabhicchada*;
*viśvarūpā*, *rūpyagaṇḍā*, *rūpya*, and *haritatumbilī*.
Arśoghna, ākhukanda, vanyakanda, and śūraṇa; raktapādī, śamīpatrā, lajjā, and lohitayaṣṭikā. (Vāgbhaṭanighaṇṭu 280)
The *durārohā*, *kharaskandhā*, and *svādumastakā* are names for the date palm (*kharjūrī*).
The *hintālī*, *mahātālī*, *kutālī*, and *tilapuṣpikā* are names for the palmyra palm (*tāla*).
The *bahuskandha*, the *mṛtyuphala*, the *gūḍhapākī*, the *śilāphalā*, the *jatuvṛkṣa*, the *ghanaskandha*, the *krimivṛkṣa*, and the *kuśāmraka*. // VAnigh_282 //
Nīlapattrī, kālanīlī, nīlinī, nīlapuṣpikā, kākajaṅghā,
dhvāṅkṣajaṅghā, dāsī, kāntā, and pracībalā.
Śarapuṅkhā, bāṇapuṅkhā, maṇikā,
cekṣupuṅkhikā, putradātrī, vṛttapattrā, vātāri, and śvetapuṣpikā.
*Tālīśapatra*, *tālīśa*, *tāla*, and *āmalakīdala* are synonyms for the *tālīśa* tree.
*Śvāsadruma*, *kākataru*, *rugyogya*, and *vyāghraparṇī* refer to the same medicinal plant suitable for treating diseases.
Kubjapuṣpā, Kṛṣṇavallī, Mahānīlā, Pratānikā, Mṛdukānti, and Mahāśvetā are synonyms; while Śvetā is known as khaṭikā (chalk).
Raktapāṣāṇaka is a mineral; girimṛd is known as gairika; that which is called stanya is dugdhapāṣāṇa; saudha is pāṣāṇaka, also known as lava.
Saugandhika and gandhaka are synonyms; vaigandha, gandhaka, and bali are also [names for fragrant substances].
Manaḥśilā, manoguptā, manohvā, kunaṭī, and śilā are synonyms for realgar.
Haritālamāla, tāla, godanta, naṭabhūṣaṇa, pārada, rasadhātu, rudraretas, and mahārasa; (these are synonyms for mercury).
Rasendra, capala, sūta, harayoni, and rasottama;
abhraka, pārvatībīja, śailodbhūta, and likewise ambara.
Mayūragrīvika is indeed tutthaka, as is śikhikaṇṭha;
another is karparikā-tuttha, and vāmana is likewise tuttha.
Hiṅgula, darada, mleccha, rasabhū, carmarañjana, sindūra, raktareṇu, śrībhūṣaṇa, and nāgasambhava; these are synonyms for vermilion.
Sauvarcala, rucaka, akṣāhva, and that known as kṛṣṇa are synonyms for salt.
Viḍa is said to be artificial (kṛtrima), while audbhida is that which originates from the earth (pṛthvīsambhava).
Sea-born (*sāmudra*) is ocean salt, also known as *paṭu*;
*yāvaśūka* is barley-alkali (*yavakṣāra*), while *srotoghnī* is *suvarcikā*.
Saubhāgya, ṭaṅkaṇa, kṣāra, that which is produced from the juice of mālatī, tāpya originating from the Tāpī river, mākṣika, and haimamākṣika; // VAnighaṇṭu 295 //
That which is produced from lac, from stone, and from mineral ore is known as *śilā* and *karpūra*;
*gorocanā*, *badarikā*, *saurāṣṭrī*, *rocanā*, and *śivā* [are synonyms].
Lākṣā, dīpti, drumavyādhi, krimijā, lohitā, and jatu are synonyms for lac.
According to Padmottara, tālakumbha, yāvaka, and alaktaka are also known as such.
Mṛganābhi, mṛgamada, kastūrī, and darpasaṃjñaka;
latākastūrikā, rālī, gandhaveṇī, and mukhapriyā [are synonyms for musk].
Ghanasāra, himarāja, karpūra, and himanāmaka are synonyms for camphor.
Mṛgasveda and mṛgajala refer to musk; pūti is known as pūtyaṇḍaja (the foul-smelling product of an egg).
Jātīphala, majjasāra, jātikā, jātipattraka, kakkolaka,
kośaphala, kolaka, and bahubījaka.
Phala, dvīpa, marīca, kaṭuka, and the fruit of kaṭukī; lavaṅga, devakusuma, kusuma, śekhara, and lava. 301.
Niṣpattra, mahāpuṣpa, svargapuṣpa, and varālaka; śilāpuṣpa, śaileya, śilāja, and likewise sthavira.
Puṣpāñjana, rītipuṣpa, and puṣpaketu are derived from rīti;
samudraphena is dried foam, while phena and vāridhija-mala are synonyms for it.
*Śaṅkha*, *vāribhava*, *kambu*, *jalaja*, and *dīrghaniḥsvana* are synonyms for conch;
*pravāla*, *vallija*, *rakta*, and *vidruma* are proclaimed as synonyms for coral.
Rūpyaka, rajata, and tāra are synonyms for silver; while suvarṇa, kanaka, jātarūpa, hema, śātakumbha, and hāṭaka are known as gold.
Jāmbūnada, hiraṇya, tapanīya, and kāñcana;
tāmra, audumbara, śulba, mihira, and that which is named harita. 306.
Rītikā, pittala, pūti, pītaloha, and saiṃhala; trapusa, that which is known as trapusa, tagara, and rūpyaśatruka. (Vāgbhaṭanighaṇṭu 307)
Lead, tin, mercury, bell-metal, brass, and ghoṣaka;
vārttāloha, vartaloha, triloha, and pañcalohaka. // VAnigh 308 //
Kṛṣṇaloha is iron; sāramāyasa is also iron; and that which arises from stone is śilodbhava.
Ayoraja is iron-dust, and loharaja is the same; it is also called kiṭṭa and ayomala.
Cipiṭa, cippaṭa, and ciṭṭa are synonyms; vālukā and sikatā are known as sand.
Lohakānta, ayaskānta, kānta, bhrāmara, and cumbaka refer to the magnet stone.
Mṛduloha (mild iron), tīkṣṇaloha (sharp iron), that which is called tīkṣṇa (sharp metal), and sūkṣmalohaka (fine metal);
kālakūṭa, mahāmusta, vatsanābha, and halāhala [are types of poison].
Vatsadantī, mahāśṛṅgī, leliha, tālapattraka,
viṣa, mūlaka, śṛṅgī, gara, and that which is known as kṛtrima (artificial poison).
Toya-cchada, vāri-parṇī, kumbhikā, and jalakumbhikā;
dīrgha-mūla, jalāvāsa, śaivāla, and jala-sambhava. (Vaiśeṣika-nighaṇṭu 313)
Paṅkaja, puṇḍarīka, śatapattra, kuśeśaya,
bisaprasūna, rājīva, jalaja, and ambhoruha are synonyms for the lotus.
Śaśipriya, Gandhāḍhya, Kumuda,
Kokanandana, Kākotpala, Kākottha, Kākākhya, and Hrasvotpala.
Their fruits are as follows: *kumbhīka*, *mūla*, *śālūka*, *kandaka*, *kaśeruka*, *sugandhi*, *sukanda*, and *mustakandaka*.
Śṛṅgāṭaka, jalaphala, jalakanda, and trikoṇaka;
karavīra, aśvamāra, bakula, and madyakesara. (Vaijayantī 317)
Alaktā, mālyaśephālī, rūpikā, tāmrapuṣpikā,
raktapuṣpī, jayā, rudrā, amlāyanī, and vanamālikā.
Āmlāyana, rājasairya, koraṇḍa, nakharañjana, tilaka, pūrṇaka, śrīmān, sudyuti, and śuklapuṣpaka. (Vaijayantī-nighaṇṭu 319)
Mālatī, sumanā, jātī, yūthikā, and gandhanāmikā;
mallikā is called vicakilā, as well as dvipuṣpī and puṣpaṭī. (Vaijayantīkośa 320)
Kuñjara, śatapattra, kaṇṭakāḍhya, kubjaka, aṭṭahāsa, and śaṅkhaśuklā— by name, it is known as śaṅkhayūthikā.
The sage Damanaka is self-controlled, disciplined, and of noble lineage;
Damanaka may also be pale-red, as is the sage Gandhotkaṭa.
Pānīya, ambu, salila, toya, udaka,
vāri, payas, kīlāla, amṛta, jīvana, bhuvana, and vana are synonyms for water.
Kṣīra, svādu, payas, dugdha, stanya, and vāri denote breast-milk; dadhi is known as māṅgalyaka, saṃtāna, and stanikā.
Ghoṣa is buttermilk struck with a stick; kālaśeya is declared to be the same.
Ghṛta, ājya, havis, and sarpiḥ refer to clarified butter; navanīta is fresh butter, and ghṛtālaya is another term for it.
Guḍa is a product of sugarcane; it is remembered as being of three kinds: khaṇḍa, phulla, and sitopalā.
Śarkarā is known as sitā, while matsyaṇḍikā is also recorded as sitā.
*Mākṣika*, *sāragha*, *kṣaudra*, *madhu*, and that which arises from the juice of flowers are synonyms for honey.
*Madhūcchiṣṭa*, *madana*, *sikthaka*, and *makṣikāmala* refer to beeswax.
Oil produced from sesame seeds, originating from sesame, is considered the best for anointing;
*prasannā* is to be known as *vāruṇī*, and it is also remembered as being fermented (*parisvinnā*).

*Kādambarī* is thick liquor; *maireya*, *āsava*, and *mada* are synonyms for intoxicant. *Mārdvīka* is to be known as honey-wine (*madhu*), while *mādhvīka* is that which is made from honey (*madhu*).
Gauḍa is made with jaggery, śārkara with white sugar, and saindhava with sugarcane juice;
khaṇḍavāsa is made with candied sugar, while paiṣṭaka is derived from flour.
Avantisoma, dhānyāmla, āranāla,
kāñjika, śukta, sauvīraka, and tuṣoda are synonyms for fermented rice-water (tuṣodaka).
Barley water, rice water, sour gruel,
fermented vinegar, *brahmāmbu*, cow’s urine, cow dung, and cow manure are thus remembered.
Śāli, vrīhi, and vara; dhānyaka, raktaśūkara, yava, sthūlamadhya, varuṇa, and munibhikṣita.
Nīvāra rice ripens without being ploughed and is the food of birds and sages;
*caṇaka* is *kalāya*, while *godhūma* (wheat) is the food of the Mlecchas.
Camasī is atibījā; koradūṣa is kodrava;
kaṅgu is that which has joints connected by nodes (saṃdhyanthisaṃbandhī); and priyaṅgu is pītataṇḍula.
Gavedhukā, gojihvā, karśanīyā, and likewise sitā;
uddālaka, known as jūrṇāhva, yāvanāla, and śukapriya. (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 336)
Kṛṣṇamudga is of the spring season, while Mādhava is produced in Surāṣṭra;
Makuṣṭha, Vanamudga, and Masūra are remedies for pitta.
Harimantha, sugandha, chickpeas with black husks,
kulattha, and kālavṛtta— these copper-colored varieties dispel wind (vāta).
The *māṣa* has a slimy juice; it is called *kuruvinda* and *vṛṣākara*.
The *rājamāṣa* is thick and slow; it is known as *khañjaka* and *kalāyaka*.
Āḍhakī is said to be tuvarī, and niṣpāvā is remembered as śimbikā;
tila is known as snehaphala, snehapūrṇa, and kṛṣṇatailaka.
The three fruits together are called *triphalā*; it is considered excellent (*varā*), superior (*śreṣṭhā*), and likewise most excellent (*uttamā*).
The root of the two [plants] is called *dvipañcamūla*, *daśamūla*, and *daśāṅghrika*.
*Trikaṭu*, *tryūṣaṇa*, *vyoṣa*, and *kaṭutraya* are said here to be the same.
*Pañcakola*, *pañcakaṭu*, *trisugandhi*, and *trijātaka* are also synonymous.
Auṣadha, bheṣaja, pathya, agada, and bhiṣagjita are terms for medicine.
Kalabha, vāraṇa, dantī, mātaṅga, dvirada, and dvipa are terms for an elephant.
The elephant is called *gaja*, *hastin*, and *karī-bha*; the female elephant is known as *kareṇu* and *hastinī*.
The horse is called * haya*, *aśva*, *turaga*, *vājī*, and *sapti*; the stallion is called *vāha* and *bāḍava*.
*Bāleya*, *rāsabha*, *jñeya*, *dhūsara*, *gardabha*, *khara*, *karabha*, *dīrghaga*, *uṣṭra*, *kṣamī*, *vesaraka*, and *balī* are synonyms for the donkey. (Vāmanapurāṇa 345)
The *śārdūla* has a variegated body, while the *vyāghra* is the *puṇḍarīka*.
The lion is the five-faced king of beasts; he is the *haryakṣa*, the *kesarī*, and the *hari*.
The lion (*kaṇṭhīrava*) is to be known as the tawny-eyed beast of prey;
among deer, the kuraṅga, vātāyu, and hariṇa are the sources of skins.
The *hariṇa* deer is copper-colored, while the *eṇa* is black and known for its soft skin;
the *kṛṣṇasāra* is the spotted deer, and the *camarī* is known for its hairy coat.
Varāha, śūkara, kīṭī, daṃṣṭrin, ghoṇī, and romaśa; stabdharoman, pṛthuskandha, kroḍa, kola, and likewise kiri are synonyms for the boar.
*Kapi*, *plavaṅga*, *plavaga*, *śākhāmṛga*,
*valīmukha*, *markaṭa*, *vānara*, *kīśa*, *vanaukā*, and *phalabhakṣaka* are synonyms for monkey.
*Śṛgāla*, *jambuka*, *kroṣṭṛ*, *gomāyu*, and *mṛgadhūrtaka* are synonyms for jackal.
*Pārāvata*, *kalarava*, *gehapakṣin*, and *kapotaka* are synonyms for pigeon.
*Kṛkavāku*, *tāmracūḍa*, *kukkuṭa*, and *caraṇāyudha* are synonyms for the cock;
*mayūra*, *barhiṇa*, *barhī*, *nīlakaṇṭha*, and *bhujaṃgabhuk* are synonyms for the peacock.
Śikhāvala, śikhin, kekī, and kalāpin denote the peacock; meghanādin denotes the cloud-cryer (peacock); ulūka denotes the owl; and vāyasāri, kauśika, and rajanīcara denote the crow's enemy (the owl).
The crow is called *kāka*, *karaṭa*, *ariṣṭa*, *balipuṣṭa*, *sakṛtpraja*,
*parabhṛt*, *balibhuj*, *dhvāṅkṣa*, *cirajīvī*, and *vāyasa*.
Ekadṛṣṭi, Ātmaghoṣa, Droṇakāka, Kṛṣṭala, Caṭaka, Kalaviṅka, Kuliṅga, and Caṭakā.
The *vijñeya*, *carmapathika*, *jātuṣa*, and *carmasāhvaya* are synonyms for the leather-footed bird (*bharadvāja*).
The *dvija*, *brāhma*, *vyāghrāṭa*, and *khañjarīṭaka* are synonyms for the wagtail.
The *sāraṅga* and the *khañjana*, the *cātaka* which lives upon the clouds,
the *vanapriya*, the *parabhṛta*, the *kokila*, the *susvara*, and the *pika*.
The tortoise is known as *gūḍhapād*, *kacchapa*, and *kūrma*; the crab is *kulīra* and *karkaṭa*.
The round shell is *śambūka* and *vṛttaśaṅkha*; the conch is *śaṅkhaka* and *mātṛgehaka*.
Mīna is a fish; aṇḍaja is also a fish; jalaukā is a leech; jalaśāyana is a water-snake;
maṇḍūka, dardura, and bheka are frogs; and kākāhi is a water-serpent.
Sarpa, pṛdāku, bhujaga, bhujaṅga, ahi, bhujaṅgama,
āśīviṣa, viṣadhara, cakrī, vyāla, and sarīsṛpa are synonyms for a snake.
Kuṇḍalī, gūḍhapād, cakṣuḥśravas, kākodara, phaṇin, darvīkara,
dīrghapṛṣṭha, jihmagas, and pavanāśana are synonyms for a serpent.
Lelihāna, daṇḍaśūka, dvijihva, bileśaya, kṛkalāsa, mayūrādī, kāleya, and bahupannaga; (these are names for snakes). 362.
Śatapād, saraṭā, cakrī, nakula, sarpabhakṣaka,
nālinī, nālahūlīkā, talāṭā, and sthūladantikā.
The *ākhūnduru* and the *mūṣaka* are known as the *vṛka* and the *dūṣaka*; the *chuchundarī*, the *rājaputrī*, and the *gandhamūṣikā* are to be understood as synonyms.
The Purohita, the Kuḍyamatsya, the Gaurī, the house-lizard,
the lizard with the form of a monitor lizard, the Prāgbāhu, and the Yugmajihvaka.
*Uṣṭra*, *biḍāla*, *mārjāra*, *vṛṣadaṃśaka*, and *ākhubhuk* denote a cat; *udaṅghā* and *kapijaṅghā* denote a mongoose; while *lohitāṅga* and *pipīlaka* denote an ant.
The earthworm, the ground-creeper, the earth-serpent, and the rain-web;
the honey-joined, the honey-maker, the honey-licker, and likewise the honey-drinker.
Dvirepha, puṣpaliḍ, bhṛṅga, ṣaṭpada, bhramara, āvali, indindira, cañcarīka, saraghā, and madhumakṣikā are synonyms for the bee.
The *lambaromā* is a fly; another is the *makṣikā*, which wards off lamps. The *pataṅgikā* is a small gnat, while the *daṃśa* is a forest fly.
The *bhṛṅgārī*, *cīrukā*, *cīrī*, *jhillikā*, and *ghargharasvanā* are names for the cricket; the *pataṃga* and *śalabha* are known as the moth; and the *svadyota* and *jyotiriṅgaṇa* are the firefly.
*Lulāya*, *mahiṣa*, *vāhadveṣin*, *kāsara*, and *sairibha* denote the buffalo. The wild ox is known as *gavaya*. *Kakudmān*, *gopati*, and *vṛṣa* denote the bull.
A bull is known as *ukṣan*, *ṛṣabha*, or *balīvarda*; a fragrant cow that protects her calf is called *surabhi*.
A cow that has calved once is a *gṛṣṭi*; a one-year-old cow is a *baṣkayaṇī*.
The essence of food is *rasa* (chyle), which is the source of blood and constitutes the firm constituent (*dhātu*).
Blood is called *rakta*, *śoṇa*, *māṃsakara*, *śoṇita*, *kṣataja*, and *asṛk*.
Pala, māṃsa, śoṇitottha, piśita, kravya, and āmiṣa are synonyms for flesh.
Picchā refers to the fat produced from flesh; vasā is the fat produced from that [picchā]. (VAnighaṇṭu 374)
Bone arises from fat and serves to bind and support the body;
marrow is the essence of bone, being the essence of oiliness produced from bone.
White light is the seed-masculinity; semen is the virile power in the final element.
Ojas, however, is the essence of the elements; it is lunar in nature and enlivens the heart.
Anila, māruta, vāyu, marut, prāṇa, prabhañjana, samīraṇa,
mātariśvan, pavana, and sadāgati are synonyms for wind.
Māyu is bile (pitta), which is fiery and hot; kapha is phlegm (śleṣman) and is slimy.
Kardama, paṅka, and jambāla denote mud; while mṛtsā, mṛtsnā, and mṛttikā denote clay.
*Hasantikā*, *aṅgāradhānī*, *tailapātra*, and *kutū* are known as synonyms for a brazier.
*Pāṣāṇa*, *prastara*, *grāvan*, *upala*, *aśman*, *śilā*, and *dṛṣat* are synonyms for stone.
Pṛthvī, Vasuṃdharā, Gaurī, Bhūmi, Medinī, Mahī, Dharā, Dharitrī, Dharaṇī, Kṣoṇī, Jyā, Kāśyapī, and Kṣiti are the names for the earth.
The earth is known as Sarvasahā, Vasumatī, Vasudhā, Urvī, Acalā, Viśvambharā, Rasā, Anantā, Gotrā, Ku, Pṛthivī, and Kṣamā.
Avanī, Bhūtadhātrī, and Vipulā; Sāgarāmbarā;
Sūra, Haṃsa, Ravi, Bhānu, Pataṅga, Arka, and Divākara.
Pradyotana, dinamaṇi, khadyota, and likewise dyumaṇi.
Bradhna, Prabhākara, Bhāsvat, Dvādaśātmā,
Divākara, Savitṛ, Sahasrāṃśu, Mārtaṇḍa, and Vikartana.
The witness of karma, the eye of the world, garlanded with rays, whose body is the triple Veda;
the fire, the lord of planets, the lord of splendors, and the lord of days.
Śītāṃśu, indu, candramas, śaśin, candra, niśākara, vidhu, sudhāṃśu, śubhrāṃśu, oṣadhīśa, and niśāpati; these are synonyms for the moon.
Abja, jaivātṛka, soma, glau, mṛgāṅka, kalānidhi,
dvijarāja, śaśadhara, nakṣatreśa, and kṣapākara are synonyms for the moon.
Aṅgāraka, Kuja, Bhauma, and Rauhiṇeya are names for Mars; Budha and Dvija are names for Mercury;
Guru, Bṛhaspati, Mantrī, Uśanas, Bhārgava, and Kavi are names for Jupiter; and Venus is known as Śukra. (Vāmanapurāṇa 388)
Śani is the lame one, the son of the Sun; Saiṃhikeya is Vidhuntuda;
Tamas is Rāhu and Svarbhānu; and Ketu is known by the name Dhvaja.
Uḍu, nakṣatra, mṛkṣa, and bha are synonyms for a lunar mansion; doṣā, nakta, niśā, kṣapā, kṣaṇadā, yāminī, rātri, triyāmā, and coravallabhā are synonyms for night.
Dina, ahani, vāsara, ghasra, and bhāskaravallabha denote a day.
Śambhu, īśa, paśupati, śiva, śūlī, and maheśvara denote Śiva.
Īśvara, Śarva, Īśāna, Śaṃkara, Candraśekhara,
Bhūteśa, Khaṇḍaparaśu, Girīśa, Giriśa, and Mṛḍa.
Conqueror of Death, clad in animal skins, wielder of the Pināka bow, Lord of the Pramathas,
the Fierce One, with matted hair, Śrīkaṇṭha, blue-throated, and bearer of the skull.
Vāmadeva, Mahādeva, Virūpākṣa, Trilocana,
Kṛśānuretas, Sarvajña, Dhūrjaṭi, and Nīlalohita.
Hara, Smarahara, Bharga, Tryambaka, Tripurāntaka,
Gaṅgādhara, Andhakaripu, Kratudhvaṃsin, and Vṛṣadhvaja.
Vyomakeśa, Bhava, Bhīma, Sthāṇu, Rudra, and Umāpati;
Umā, Kātyāyanī, Gaurī, Kālī, and Haimavatīśvarī.
Śivā, Aparṇā, Bhavānī, Pārvatī, Caṇḍikā, and Ambikā; Aja, Hari, Vāsudeva, Daityāri, and Puruṣottama.
Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Vaikuṇṭha, Viṣṭaraśravas,
Dāmodara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Keśava, Mādhava, and Svabhū.
Pītāmbara, Acyuta, Śārṅgin, Viṣvaksena,
Janārdana, Upendra, Indrāvaraja, Cakrapāṇi, and Caturbhuja.
Lakṣmī, Padmālayā, Padmā, Kamalā, Śrī, Haripriyā, Indirā, Lokamātā, Mā, Kṣīrābdhitanayā, and Ramā. (Vaiśyanighaṇṭu 400)
*Netra*, *pāda*, *śiphā*, and *aṅghri* refer to the root; *mūla*, *śālūka*, and *kandaka* refer to the bulbous root.
*Tvak*, *carma*, and *valkala* are said to mean the bark; *viṭapa*, *śikhara*, and *śiras* refer to the top or crown of a tree.
*Pattra*, *dala*, *chada*, *parṇa*, *palāśa*, and *chadana* are synonyms for leaf.
*Pallava* and *pravāla* refer to a sprout, while *mukula* and *koraka* are known as a bud.
*kalikā*, *jālaka*, *koraka*, *kṣāraka*, and *kuḍmala*; as well as *prasūna*, *sumanas*, *sūna*, *puṣpa*, and *kusuma* are known as synonyms for a flower.
That which is unripe is designated as *śalāṭu*, while that which is ripe is called *phala*.
*Makaranda* is the nectar of flowers; it is the juice arising from petals, the essence produced from leaves.
Auṣadha, bheṣaja, pathya, agada, and bhiṣagjita; kriyā, cikitsita, śastra, and prāyaścitta are used as synonyms for medical treatment. 405.
He is the remover of disease, the maker of medicine, the physician, the healer, the practitioner of medicine;
he is the knower of diseases, the giver of life, the wise one, the knower of the science of longevity (Āyurveda), and the destroyer of ailments.
May Dhanvantari— who is endowed with the nectar and the splendor of the cool-rayed moon, who is possessed of wealth,
and who is born from the Ocean of Milk as the lotus-born one— protect you.
May the two Aśvins, the Nāsatyas, the wonder-workers, and both their sons, the Aśvinīkumāras—
those physicians of the gods— protect the sons of physicians with their own radiant splendor.
